text: {"voice_profile":"Brisk, comic-thriller third person in a light, ironic 1920s register. In Tuppence's scenes the narrator sits close to her thoughts, wryly reporting her self-congratulation ('intoxicated with the success of truthfulness'), her money-mindedness and her schoolgirl slang. In Tommy's scenes the voice turns slow, practical and understated: he weighs his options, admits to nerves and feels plain indignation ('What a dirty trick!'). Comedy and menace alternate quickly. Short dialogue exchanges carry the plot. Villains give themselves away through tics: snarling, sibilance, heel-clicking. The narrator often inserts small ironic asides and callbacks such as buns, hospital plates and the terrier shake. Characters guess at identities by voice and appearance rather than knowing them.","book_context":"Tommy and Tuppence are two demobilised, penniless young people who form the 'Young Adventurers, Ltd.' and blunder into a hunt for Jane Finn and a lost draft treaty. Behind the plot is the unseen 'Mr. Brown', whose rule is to stay as an unnoticed nonentity in the background. The book plants small clues that pay off later: a clerk addressed as Brown, the name Rita, a password, faces that seem familiar, the date of the 29th, a curtained recess, a portrait of the pale Russian. Ignorance is played as accidental bluff: Tuppence 'knows' only a name, and Tommy later fakes knowledge. Chapter II begins the main plot through Tuppence's chance use of 'Jane Finn'. Chapter VIII shows the conspiracy's inner council as overheard fragments, ending on a cliffhanger. Keep his description: big, clean-shaven, heavy jowl, small shifty cunning eyes.","He admits overhearing the Lyons' conversation and following her, gives his card (Mr. Edward Whittington, Esthonia Glassware Co., city office), and sets an eleven o'clock appointment. Tuppence accepts.","Tuppence's private resolve, ending with her catchphrase. Keep her terrier-like shake of the shoulders.","The office has a small, rather dirty outer office with a middle-aged clerk who shows her in. Do not add a telephone to the outer office.","The offer: £100 down plus expenses for a 'nominal' trip to Paris. She would enter Madame Colombier's pensionnat for possibly three months, as his ward, with no communication with friends and absolute secrecy. He suggests she pass as an American because of her slight accent picked up from an American hospital friend.","Tuppence objects that the terms are too liberal. He replies that he is paying for intelligence and for discretion not to ask questions. She insists on 'both or neither' for her partner Mr. Beresford and rises to leave.","Asked her name, she shields the archdeacon by saying 'Jane Finn', which she believes she has invented. Whittington turns purple with rage and dismay and accuses her of cat-and-mouse play.","The bluff by truthfulness: 'Rita knows nothing about me'; 'Very little indeed'; 'It might be my own name'; 'hit upon it by chance'. Show that her truthful denials increase his unease.","'How much do you want?' tempts her after a breakfast and supper of buns. She claims to live by her wits and asks for 'a little something down'. He calls it blackmail; she calls it payment for services in advance. He grudgingly admires her.","The clerk knocks and brings a 'telephone message'. Whittington frowns, says 'That'll do, Brown', abruptly dismisses her with £50 and tells her to come tomorrow. He reasons that 'Mr. Brown' is a password and that entering the meeting room unknown would be foolhardy, then hides in the curtained recess opposite the door, which also overlooks the stairs.","The arrivals, each giving the signal knock: a brutish criminal who answers 'Fourteen' to the bearded, precise-voiced man ('Your number, comrade?'), whom Tommy takes for a German; an Irish Sinn Feiner; a shabby clerk-like man; a working man whose face seems vaguely familiar; and a commanding, well-born man whose face Tommy also half knows but cannot name. Keep the variety, which shows the organisation's reach.","The last arrival is small, pale and gentle-mannered, with Slavonic cheekbones and strange light eyes that seem to see through the curtain. Everyone rises for him. He asks whether Mr. Brown is present and is told only a 'message' has come. He suggests Brown may be among them, and the men eye one another. He is seated as 'Number One'. Number Fourteen shuts the door.","Tommy, shoeless, finds the door locked or bolted. He carefully restores the handle and expresses indignation, then shows his bulldog tenacity: he enters the adjoining bedroom, draws the rusty bolt of the communicating door and listens through a portière. He can hear but not see, so identify speakers only by voice ('rather thought was that of Boris').","Overheard business: the Sinn Feiner demands money for a reign of terror in Ireland. Number One grants it and tells Boris to see to it. The commanding man makes the Belfast quip. There is a loan to an English newspaper, with a Moscow denial if needed. The German reports on the unions 'directed by--Mr. Brown'.","The date of the 29th, set by the Labour leaders, who must believe the strike is their own show. Keep Number One's 'honest men' remarks.","'Clymes must go', assigned to Number Fourteen, with the promise of legal defence and gloves bearing a housebreaker's fingerprints. Keep Fourteen's relish for blood and for jewels in the gutter.","The German admits doubt that the leaders will strike. A certain document would ensure success, but they do not have it and do not know where it is. Perhaps one person knows: a girl. 'This case is different.'
